content: Approximately one-quarter of individuals will experience a mental disorder at some point in their lives. Despite the high prevalence and significant negative consequences of mental disorders, many individuals remain undiagnosed or do not receive adequate treatment. Primary health care has been recognized as a critical component in improving the delivery of mental health care. Consultation liaison is a model of mental health care in which the primary care provider retains the central role in managing mental health care, while a mental health specialist offers consultative support. This approach has the potential to enhance the quality of mental health care provided in primary care settings, ultimately improving outcomes for individuals with mental disorders. The objective of this study was to determine whether consultation liaison can positively impact individuals with mental disorders by enhancing the ability of primary care providers to deliver mental health care. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in March 2014 across multiple databases, including the EPOC Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. Reference lists of relevant studies and reviews were also examined to identify additional studies. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared consultation liaison to standard care or other mental health care service models in primary care settings. Participants included individuals attending primary care practices who required mental health care or had a mental disorder, as well as primary care providers directly involved in delivering mental health care. Two independent reviewers screened the identified studies against inclusion criteria and extracted data on study design, participants, interventions, outcomes, and potential biases. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Trial authors were contacted to obtain missing information. Data were analyzed for follow-up periods of up to three months, between three and 12 months, and beyond 12 months after the start of treatment. A random-effects model was used to calculate risk differences (RD) for binary outcomes and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB). For continuous data, mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) were calculated. The search identified 8,203 citations, of which 12 trials met the inclusion criteria. These trials involved 2,605 consumer participants and over 905 primary care practitioners. Eleven trials compared consultation liaison to standard care, while one trial compared it to collaborative care, where a case manager coordinated mental health care. Eight trials focused on individuals with depression, while the remaining trials included participants with various disorders such as anxiety, somatoform disorders, medically unexplained symptoms, and alcohol-related problems. None of the trials provided separate data for children or older adults. There was some evidence that consultation liaison improved mental health outcomes within three months of treatment initiation (two trials, n = 445, NNTB 8, 95% CI 5 to 25). However, there was no evidence of its effectiveness between three and 12 months. Consultation liaison also appeared to enhance consumer satisfaction (up to three months: one trial, n = 228, NNTB 3, 95% CI 3 to 5; three to 12 months: two trials, n = 445, NNTB 8, 95% CI 5 to 17) and adherence to treatment (three to 12 months: seven trials, n = 1,251, NNTB 6, 95% CI 4 to 13) for up to 12 months. Primary care providers demonstrated improved outcomes in delivering adequate treatment between three and 12 months (three trials, n = 797, NNTB 7, 95% CI 4 to 17) and in prescribing pharmacological treatments for up to 12 months (four trials, n = 796, NNTB 13, 95% CI 7 to 50). However, there was some evidence suggesting that consultation liaison may be less effective than collaborative care in addressing mental disorder symptoms, disability, general health status, and treatment provision. The quality of evidence was generally low for all outcomes, except for consumer adherence between three and 12 months, which was rated as moderate quality. Eight trials were deemed to have a high risk of performance bias, as participants were likely aware of their group allocation, and most outcomes were self-reported. Attrition bias was rated high in eight trials, and reporting bias was high in six trials. In conclusion, consultation liaison appears to improve mental health outcomes for up to three months and enhances satisfaction and adherence to treatment for up to 12 months in individuals with mental disorders, particularly depression. Primary care providers were more likely to deliver adequate treatment and prescribe pharmacological therapy for up to 12 months. However, consultation liaison may be less effective than collaborative care in certain areas, such as symptom management and general health outcomes. The overall quality of the evidence was low, and further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of consultation liaison, particularly for mental disorders other than depression.
